permitName: Bryce Canyon National Park Backcountry Permits

description.cancellation_policy:
Cancellation Policy: Reservations cancelled 3 or more full days before the reservation start date receive a full refund of the recreation fee. ($5.00 per-person fee)

Reservations cancelled less than 3 days before the permit start date are non-refundable.

The $10 reservation fee is non-refundable. 

Change Policy: You may make changes to your permit itinerary, if space is available, up until you claim your permit. 

  • Your start date cannot be changed without cancelling your existing reservation and booking a new reservation.
  • If the group size is increased (quota permitting), you will be required to pay the additional per person fees.
  • If the group size is reduced more than 3 days before the permit start date, a refund of the per person fees will be provided.

One additional permit holder can be identified when the reservation is created. Otherwise, reservations and permits are non-transferable.
description.description:
Bryce Canyon National Park is best known for its hoodoos--intricately carved rock spires left standing through the processes of weathering and erosion. Hoodoos are best experienced through day hikes in the main amphitheater of Bryce Canyon. The backcountry trails of Bryce Canyon offer forests, meadows, stunning views of distant cliffs, wildflowers, wildlife, interesting geologic features and solitude, but few hoodoos. 

There are two backcountry trails at Bryce Canyon, the Under-the-Rim Trail and Riggs Spring Loop Trail. Both descend below the rim into a piñon-juniper-ponderosa forest. The trails are strenuous, with multiple changes in elevation. Both trails may be hiked either direction.

Elevation ranges from 6,800 to 9,115 feet (2073 to 2778 m).

Under-the-Rim Trail

The Under-the-Rim Trail is approximately 22.9 miles (7 km) from Bryce Point to Rainbow Point. Three connecting trails intersect the Under-the-Rim trail at Swamp Canyon, Whiteman Bench, and Agua Canyon trailheads. Agua Canyon Connecting trail is currently closed. There are seven campsites along the Under-the-Rim Trail.

The Under-the-Rim trail can be broken up into the following sections:

Bryce Point Trailhead to Swamp Canyon Trailhead

Distance: 11.6 mi (18.7 km) / Elevation change: 1294 ft (349 m)

Steep descent from Bryce Point through Hat Shop to Yellow Creek through juniper forests and gambel oak thickets. Hike through some sandy areas.

Swamp Canyon Trailhead to Whiteman Bench Trailhead

Distance: 3.6 mi (5.8 km) / Elevation change: 848 ft (259 m)

Hike through plant communities. Excellent views across southeastern Utah and into northern Arizona. 

Whiteman Bench Trailhead to Rainbow Point Trailhead

Distance: 11.7 mi (18.7 km) / Elevation change: 1460 ft (445 m)

Hike through interesting geology. This section of trail is known for rough terrain, but beautiful scenery and some sandy areas. Hike up and down ridges. Ponderosa pines yield to spruce, fir and aspen. Steep climb to Rainbow Point.

Riggs Spring Loop Trail

The Riggs Spring Loop Trail is an 8.6-mile (14 km) loop, which begins and ends at the Rainbow/ Yovimpa Point trailheads. This trail descends to the valley below the cliffs at the south end of the park, through ponderosa pine, fir, aspen, maple, and gambel oak. There are four campsites along the Riggs Spring Loop Trail.
description.driving_directions:
From the North: Take I-15 south to UT-20 (exit 95). Travel east on UT-20 to US-89. Follow US-89 south to UT-12. Travel east on UT-12 to UT-63. Take UT-63 south to Bryce Canyon NP.

From the South through Zion National Park: Take I-15 north to UT-9 (exit 16). Follow UT-9 east through Zion National Park to US-89. Travel north on US-89 to UT-12. Go east on UT-12 to UT-63. Take UT-63 south to Bryce Canyon NP. From the East Travel west on UT-12 to UT-63. Take UT-63 south to Bryce Canyon NP.

Backcountry permits must be picked up at the Bryce Canyon Visitor Center located immediately past the entrance station on the right (west) side of UT-63.
description.fee_policy:
Permit Reservation Fee: $10.00 non-refundable reservation fee. 

Recreation Fee: $5 per each person listed on the permit. The recreation fee is charged year-round for permits secured through recreation.gov or in person at the Bryce Canyon Visitor Center. This fee is refundable up to 3 days before permit start date. 

Entrance Fee. An entrance fee, separate from the fees above, is required for all visitors to the park. You may pay upon arrival or pay in advance. The park also honors Federal interagency passes (e.g., annual, senior, access, military, 4th grade, Golden Age pass etc.). For more information visit the park's Fees & Passes page.
description.need_to_know_email:
• This confirmation email is not your permit. Pick up your permit at the visitor center starting 2 days before but no later than 1 hour before the visitor center closes on your trip start date. 
  • Check Bryce Canyon's weather forecast, Flash Flood and Lightning Safety Information before you go.
  • Bryce Canyon DOES NOT offer shuttle service to or from Rainbow Point. Visit the park's Commercial Tours and Services page for providers.   
  • Carry a topo map and compass and know how to use them. The Under-the-Rim Trail is rugged and can be difficult to follow.   
  • Pets and vehicles (including bicycles) are prohibited.
  • Use designated campsites and designated trails only.
  • Carry a minimum of 1 gallon (4 liters) of water per day per person. Water sources are unreliable. Treat backcountry water by filtering, boiling for 10 minutes, or using iodine. Check current water source information at the visitor center. 
  • The park requires bear-resistant canisters. The visitor center will loan free canisters. If you own a hard-sided and lockable bear-resistant canister, you must present it to the rangers for compliance. Use bear-resistant canisters for food and ANY aromatic items (soap, lip balm, lotion, etc.). Keep it in the canister unless you’re using it, cooking it or eating it. Place bear canister 100 yards downwind and downhill from your tent to ensure the canister rolls AWAY FROM your tent.  
  • Follow Leave No Trace Principles.
  • Don’t feed, approach, or bother wildlife. The NPS Staying Safe Around Bears page describes what to do if you encounter a bear.  
  • Pack out all trash, including toilet paper and food scraps.
  • Bury human waste. Bury 6-8 in (15-20 cm) deep, and at least 200 ft (60 m) from water, trails and campsites.  
  • NO OPEN FIRES. Use a camp stove.  
  • Trees. Don’t hang anything (e.g., hammocks) from the trees.  
  • Cancellation: The $10.00 reservation fee is non-refundable. The $5 per person recreation fee is refundable up to 3 days before the start date.
description.need_to_know_order:
• Be safe. Carry a topographic map and let a friend or family member know your plans.
  • Check the weather. Be aware of flash floods and lightning hazards (in case of lightning stay down below the rim and away from isolated trees)
  • Check water availability. PURIFY all water from backcountry sources.   
  • Camp in designated backcountry campsites only. 
  • NO OPEN FIRES. Use camp stoves instead. 
  • Do not hang anything from the trees, including hammocks.
  • Bury human waste 6-8 in (15-20 cm) deep, and at least 200 ft (60 m) from water, trails and campsites.
  • Pack out all trash, including toilet paper and food scraps.
  • Pets of any kind, and vehicles (including bicycles) are prohibited.
  • Don’t feed, approach, or bother wildlife- you are the visitor encrouching on THEIR environment. Stay safe around bears 
  • Use wildlife resistant canisters to store food and ANY other aromatic items (soap, chapstick, lotion…) Bear-resistant canisters are available for loan, free of charge at the visitor center. If you have your own bear-resistant canister, you must present it to the ranger to make sure it meets park requirements (hard-sided and lockable). Please educate yourself on bear awareness.
  • If you’re not using it, cooking it, or eating it, it stays in the canister – place bear canister 100 yards downwind and downhill from your tent, so if canister rolls it rolls AWAY FROM your tent.
  • LEAVE NO TRACE of your passing. Hike on designated trails.
description.need_to_know_permit:
Your reservation is not a permit. Permits must be issued in person at the Bryce Canyon Visitor Center within two days of your trip start date, but no later than 1 hour before the visitor center closes on your trip start date.

An entrance fee, separate from the permit fee, is required for all backcountry campers entering the park. You may pay upon arrival or pay in advance. The park also honors Federal interagency passes (e.g., annual, senior, access, military, 4th grade, Golden Age pass etc.). For more information visit the park's Fees & Passes page. 

Conditions along the Under-the-Rim Trail are very rugged, and the trail may be difficult to follow. Orienteering skills are strongly recommended. Please carry a topographic map and compass.

Water sources in the backcountry are intermittent and unreliable. Water may be found in Yellow Creek, Sheep Creek, Swamp Creek, Iron Spring, Riggs Spring, and Yovimpa Spring. However, because water sources are unreliable, we recommend you carry at least one gallon (4 liters) of water per day per person. You may encounter large stretches of trail without access to water sources. Water from backcountry sources must be purified by boiling 10 minutes, filtering, or iodine treatment. Current information on water sources is available at the visitor center. 

Bryce Canyon National Park does not provide a shuttle or transportation to/from Rainbow Point. You must provide your own options for transportation. For alternate options visit our Commercial Tours and Services page. 

Bear-resistant canisters are required on overnight backcountry hikes. Bryce Canyon is home to many animals including mountain lions, coyotes and black bears. Squirrels, snakes and other small animals may also be present near your campsite. Canisters are available for loan, free of charge at the visitor center. If you have your own bear-resistant canister, you must present it to the ranger to make sure it meets park requirements (hard-sided and lockable). 

The following regulations and recommendations are also in place:

  • Store all food and scented personal items in the bear canister
  • Do not eat or use scented items in your tent
  • Do not sleep in clothes you were wearing when you cooked
  • Keep bear canisters locked when not tending to them
  • Hanging food from trees is prohibited

In the summer of 2010, a black bear had to be killed because it was conditioned to associate food with humans and began to exhibit aggressive behavior. Feeding wild animals is a form of animal cruelty. Please take your food storage practices seriously. Stay safe around bears 

Cell service is very limited. Cellular phones may work in some areas but should not be relied on.

Lightning is a year-round danger, though most common in July, August and September. During the rainy (monsoon) season expect frequent, usually brief, afternoon thunderstorms which produce heavy rain and frequent lightning. If you are planning your trip during these months remember that in the backcountry there may not be a safe place to take shelter.

Winter camping requires appropriate equipment and knowledge of basic winter survival skills. Backcountry trails are not marked for winter use and can be extremely difficult to find when snow covered. During snowstorms, UT-63 is temporarily closed from mile 4 to Rainbow Point until it is plowed. This affects all backcountry trailheads except Bryce Point.
description.no_show_policy: No Show Policy: All permits must be issued in person during the Bryce Canyon Visitor Center hours of operation (8:00 a.m.-6:00 p.m. summer/ 8:00 a.m. - 4:30 p.m. winter). The permit holder shall pick up their permit no later than 1 hour before the visitor center closes on their reservation start date. If the permit holder fails to show up, the reservation will be cancelled. No Shows are non-refundable.
description.quota_details:
Bryce Canyon's backcountry trails and campsites are located within the park's Recommended Wilderness Area, which is managed to protect its wilderness character. Naturalness and opportunities for solitude are important components of this character. 

To minimize the impact on park resources, backcountry camping is restricted to designated campsites.

Each backcountry campsite has 3 tent pads which is limited to 3 groups totaling no more than 6 people. 

Backcountry group campsites are limited to 15 people. 

A permit allows for up to 14 consecutive nights. Backpackers may stay up to 2 consecutive nights in any campsite. Water is very limited in the backcountry and often sets the number of nights for a trip. On average campers spend 1-3 nights in Bryce Canyon’s backcountry. 

The permit is valid only for the number of people, dates and locations indicated.
description.season_information:
A permit is required year-round for all overnight stays in the backcountry. A backcountry permit allows the permit holder and their group to camp in designated backcountry campsites.

  • Permits for March 1 through November 30, become available for reservation 3 months in advance of today’s date.

  • Permits for winter backcountry camping, December 1 through the last day of February are only available in person at the Bryce Canyon Visitor Center. (Winter backcountry permits are not available through recreation.gov).

  • After making your online backcountry reservation, you must meet with a ranger at the Bryce Canyon Visitor Center to obtain your physical backcountry permit.

  • Permits must be picked up in person at least one hour before the visitor center closes on the day of your trip or your reservation will be cancelled.
